hypothesis_tracker.H1: refuted — aggregate is flat but that masks divergent subgroups
hypothesis_tracker.H2: strongly supported — user-type mix shift + divergent rates is Simpson's Paradox
hypothesis_tracker.H3: partially supported — paid visits slightly down but organic up; paid not degrading faster than others
hypothesis_tracker.H4: supported — new-user conv rate up +2.13pp; returning down -3.88pp
hypothesis_tracker.H5: refuted — post-signup (s->c) is stable; movement is at visit-to-signup

findings.claim: Aggregate visit-to-conversion rate is genuinely flat (8.67% Jan -> 8.76% Jun, slope +0.021pp/mo, r^2=0.028, p=0.75). The 'nothing is wrong' headline is arithmetically correct.
findings.evidence: Overall groupby('month').sum() then conversions/visits. Linear regression on 6 monthly values.

findings.claim: New-user conversion rate climbed +2.13pp (5.24% -> 7.37%, +40.6% relative) with a statistically significant upward slope (+0.43pp/mo, r^2=0.94, p=0.0014).
Returning-user conversion rate fell -3.88pp (13.81% -> 9.93%, -28.1% relative) with a statistically significant downward slope (-0.78pp/mo, r^2=0.97, p=0.0003).
findings.evidence: Same pivot as F2. linregress on returning user conv rate.

validation.robustness: slope -0.74 to -0.84pp/mo across all 6 leave-one-out runs

findings.claim: Visit-mix shifted from 60% new / 40% returning in Jan to 46% new / 54% returning in Jun. With rising returning share and falling returning conv rate, a textbook Simpson's Paradox masks the divergence.
findings.evidence: Jun conv rate if Jun user_type mix had held Jan's subgroup rates = 9.88% vs actual 8.76%; if mix had stayed at Jan's shares (with Jun rates) = 8.39%. Subgroup divergence is real and opposite in direction.

methods: counterfactual decomposition (Jan mix x Jun rates, Jun mix x Jan rates)
validation.notes: Simpson's Paradox confirmed; pattern also holds WITHIN each channel

findings.claim: Pattern holds across every channel: in paid_search, organic, email, and referral, new-user conversion rose +1.87 to +2.45pp and returning-user conversion fell -2.71 to -5.11pp. This is not channel-specific — it is systemic to user-type.
findings.evidence: groupby(['month','channel','user_type']).sum() pivot; compare Jan vs Jun v2c for each cell.

findings.claim: The entire movement — both the new-user gain and the returning-user decline — is at the visit-to-signup step. Post-signup efficiency (signup-to-conversion) is stable for both user types (new: 60.1% -> 59.7%; returning: 50.9% -> 51.4%).
findings.evidence: By user_type, compute signups/visits and conversions/signups monthly. New v->s: +3.62pp; new s->c: -0.40pp. Returning v->s: -7.81pp; returning s->c: +0.50pp.

methods: chain-rule check: v2c == v2s * s2c for all 48 cells, max diff 1.4e-17

findings.claim: Traffic mix also shifted: new-user visits fell ~22% across every channel (paid_search -24%, organic -22%, email -21%, referral -21%) while returning-user visits rose 28-44% (organic +44%, referral +41%, paid_search +34%, email +28%). Total visits are effectively flat; the composition changed.
findings.evidence: groupby(['month','channel','user_type']).visits.sum(). Compare Jan vs Jun per cell.

validation.notes: compositional shift, not a lost-traffic story — total visits flat

findings.claim: Opportunity sizing: if returning-user conv rate had held at Jan's 13.81% in June, we would have converted ~1,187 more returning users in June alone (~14,240/yr at current returning volume). If June had kept Jan's new-user volume at June's improved 7.37% rate, we would have converted ~569 additional new users that month.
findings.evidence: Counterfactual: 30,564 June returning visits x (13.81% - 9.93%) = 1,187 missed conversions. 33,583 Jan new visits x 7.37% vs actual 1,906 = +569.

validation.notes: arithmetic verified; causal assumption about reversibility is unprovable from 6 months of data
validation.caveat: assumes returning-user decline is reversible and new-user gains would have held at higher volume
